text: Layer 1C universe should track AI infrastructure as a relay of constraints: accelerator demand drives HBM, advanced packaging, test, optics, rack power, cooling, grid interconnection, construction services, and system integration.
HBM-adjacent test and IP names such as FORM, RMBS, and COHU currently have the strongest underfollowed evidence in the visible Layer 1B context.

Optics/photonics remains a high-potential Serenity discovery lane, but Layer 2 must separate factual AI datacenter exposure from speculative social-media narratives around AXTI, AAOI, SIVE, and related names.

Rack power, thermal management, switchgear, electrical components, and grid interconnection should remain in the universe even where company evidence is incomplete because they may become deployment bottlenecks after chip supply improves.

Next layer should run primary-source checks on every underfollowed candidate: latest 10-K/10-Q, earnings transcripts, investor decks, customer concentration, backlog, capacity, revenue segment exposure, and valuation/pricing checks.

Current merged universe is US-public-market biased; future passes should add Taiwan, Japan, Korea, Europe, Hong Kong, and A-share mappings for substrates, packaging tools, memory test, transformers, liquid cooling, and optical components.

Track AI infrastructure as a physical constraint relay: demand capex -> accelerators -> leading-edge wafers -> HBM -> advanced packaging -> test/inspection -> optics -> rack power/cooling -> data-center electrical systems -> grid interconnection.

Highest-confidence chokepoint nodes for Layer 2A are advanced packaging, HBM stack/interface/test, 800G/1.6T optics, direct liquid cooling, large power transformers, switchgear, and utility interconnection.

Low-attention value may hide in probe cards, metrology, wafer-level burn-in, HBM interface IP, InP substrates, lasers, optical DSPs, contract optical manufacturing, cold plates, CDUs, power modules, busbars, switchgear, transformers, permitting specialists, and commissioning services.

Key catalysts to monitor: hyperscaler capex updates, TSMC CoWoS/3DFabric capacity commentary, HBM3E/HBM4 qualification, 1.6T optical deployment, liquid-cooled rack rollouts, utility interconnection reform, transformer lead-time updates, and onsite-power/microgrid policy.

Layer 2B should verify which public suppliers have material revenue exposure, named customer wins, capacity constraints, backlog visibility, customer qualification, and pricing power at each bottleneck node.

Do not over-map the theme to high-attention leaders only. Need to separately validate underfollowed suppliers in test, photonics materials, power conversion, switchgear, transformers, liquid cooling, and commissioning.

FORM maps most directly to the HBM / advanced-packaging test-gate node via probe cards and known-good-die validation, but the next layer must verify HBM mix, backlog, customer concentration, and margin accretion from primary filings.

RMBS maps to the HBM interface-IP / PHY / memory-controller toll-road node; current support is inferential and must be upgraded only if HBM3E/HBM4 design wins, license economics, or volume-linked sensitivity are verified.
COHU maps to HBM inspection, metrology, thermal handling, and advanced-package test automation; survival in Layer 3 depends on repeat orders and material revenue contribution.

AXTI remains a speculative_shadow InP substrate / specialty-material candidate for AI photonics and external-light-source architectures; primary filing verification is mandatory because current evidence is thesis-context-heavy.

AEHR remains a speculative_shadow reliability / wafer-level burn-in candidate; the key gating evidence is direct AI, photonics, accelerator, or advanced-packaging test demand beyond legacy cyclical drivers.
AMKR maps to the OSAT / heterogeneous integration / advanced-packaging capacity layer, but AI materiality is not yet proven from the provided evidence.
AAOI maps to datacenter optical networking and potential 800G/1.6T transceiver demand; it remains speculative until datacenter AI revenue mix, customers, capacity, and margins are verified.
SIVE maps to external-light-source / photonics components as a niche speculative_shadow candidate; evidence must show named customers, volume timing, revenue scale, and funding runway.
FN maps to optical-module contract manufacturing and qualification, where AI optical volume may appear through branded customer ramps rather than direct AI labeling.
COHR maps to optics, lasers, and compound-semiconductor components as a reference-to-underfollowed hybrid; direct AI datacenter mix and laser supply tightness need primary verification.

Layer 2B still lacks live filing-level verification for FORM, COHU, AEHR, AMKR, AAOI, SIVE, FN, and COHR. Do not upgrade these beyond current claim labels until filings, transcripts, customer announcements, or product disclosures confirm AI/HBM/800G/1.6T/ELS materiality.

Market-pricing checks are still missing for the chunk: market capitalization, revenue growth expectations, valuation, short interest, analyst coverage, and whether each name is already crowded by AI-photonics or HBM narratives.

MOD has explicit data-center cooling exposure supported by annual-report evidence and Airedale by Modine product announcements; keep as a stronger underfollowed cooling candidate but verify revenue mix, backlog, capacity, and liquid-cooling share.

NVT maps to AI data-center liquid cooling, racks, power distribution, and connection products; evidence includes data-solutions materials and liquid-cooling product launch, but organic growth and customer materiality need filing-level verification.

CLS has one of the cleanest explicit relationships in this chunk to AI/cloud data-center infrastructure through CCS products including switches, optical systems, racks, servers, and storage for AI workloads.
IESC has strong underfollowed services exposure: fiscal 2025 filings cite data-center demand, record Communications backlog, and Q1 FY2026 revenue growth driven by data centers.
SMTC maps to 1.6T AI data-center optics via PMD, VCSEL driver, TIA, and optical/copper connectivity; next work should quantify revenue and design-win durability.

SANM relationship upgraded from hypothesis to fact for cloud/AI infrastructure manufacturing because fiscal 2025 materials cite ZT Systems data-center infrastructure manufacturing acquisition and cloud/AI infrastructure end-market strength.
VICR remains a plausible rack/board power candidate, but gathered evidence only proves exposure to enterprise/HPC and network infrastructure markets, not specific AI accelerator platform wins.
BELFB remains a messy-label component hypothesis; evidence supports power/protection/connectivity segments but not yet direct AI data-center content, customer wins, or component content per rack.

ATKR has data-center construction-component relevance through conduit/fittings/cable-management products, but AI-specific materiality is unproven and pricing/commodity cyclicality must be checked before it survives later layers.
APG has broad inspection/service/monitoring evidence but lacks explicit gathered proof of data-center or AI-data-center revenue; keep only as a low-confidence facility-services hypothesis.

PWR should remain a reference anchor for grid interconnection and transmission rather than the main underfollowed alpha lane; evidence supports data-center customer power opportunities but the company is already high-attention and large-cap.

VRT remains a reference anchor for AI data-center thermal and power infrastructure; relationship is evidence-backed, but alpha relevance requires backlog, liquid-cooling revenue, capacity, and valuation checks.
ETN remains a reference anchor for data-center electrical distribution and switchgear demand; official Q1 2026 disclosure supports data-center-driven order/backlog momentum.
MU is a reference HBM supplier for AI accelerator memory stacks; HBM3E/HBM4 transition should be tracked through revenue allocation, qualification, supply commitments, and margin evidence.
TSM is the advanced-packaging/foundry benchmark for the theme; CoWoS/InFO/SoIC capacity disclosures should be used to relay constraints toward substrates, OSATs, test, and tooling candidates.
NVDA is not an underfollowed target but is the architecture anchor: rack-scale liquid cooling, power shelves, busbars, NVLink cabling, and HBM content define downstream supplier research nodes.
AVGO is a reference anchor for custom AI ASICs and Ethernet networking; OpenAI collaboration evidence supports demand mapping for advanced packaging, optics, and networking supply-chain nodes.
ANET is a reference anchor for AI Ethernet networking; use it to monitor scale-up/scale-out Ethernet adoption and related optical-component demand rather than as the primary underfollowed hunt.

FLEX upgraded from Layer-1 hypothesis to evidence-backed underfollowed relationship for AI/cloud data-center power, cooling, rack integration, and infrastructure manufacturing; still needs segment economics and customer validation.

JBL upgraded from Layer-1 hypothesis to evidence-backed underfollowed relationship for AI/cloud data-center EMS, servers, infrastructure, liquid-cooling, and power-management adjacency; still needs revenue/margin/customer validation.
RPI should remain speculative_shadow only: official evidence supports embedded/industrial/OEM computing exposure, not material AI infrastructure supply-chain exposure.
For FLEX and JBL, later layers must verify whether AI infrastructure is material to consolidated revenue and margins rather than merely a product-page or press-release exposure.

For all high-attention reference names, Layer 2C should add market-pricing checks: valuation, expected growth embedded in consensus, analyst coverage, short interest where relevant, and whether bottleneck narratives are already crowded.

This chunk is reference-heavy; the next Serenity pass should deliberately branch from NVDA/TSM/MU/AVGO/ANET/VRT/ETN toward smaller component, tool, test, substrate, cooling, power-module, busbar, CDU, and service suppliers.
